title: Electro-Thermal Origins of Enhanced Performance and Scalability in Disc-Type Phase-Change Memory
authors: Ghazi Sarwat Syed, Loris Coccia, Siddharth Gautam, Vara Prasad Jonnalagadda, Abu Sebastian
abstract: Disc-type phase-change memory is a promising device architecture for analog in-memory computing, enabled by the unique physical properties of ultra-thin phase-change materials and the device geometry. In this study, we develop a comparative analytical framework using compact electro-thermal models to examine the state dependent readout and programming behavior of these devices. The framework provides insight into the fundamental physical mechanisms responsible for their enhanced functionality and highlights promising directions for further device optimization and performance improvement.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive electro-thermal analysis of disc-type Phase-Change Memory, positioning it as a leading candidate for analog in-memory computing. Using compact analytical models, the authors demonstrate that the disc geometry mitigates variability and achieves superior scaling compared to conventional PCM designs. The work provides critical insights into optimizing device operation by understanding the underlying thermal and resistive physics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the energy consumption and latency challenges in AI algorithms by analyzing the performance and scalability of disc-type Phase-Change Memory (PCM) for Analog In-Memory Computing (IMC).
main_result: Disc-type PCM devices are shown to offer advantages over dome-type geometries, enabling low programming currents and maintaining favorable scaling properties due to their geometry's resistance to variability.
method: The study develops and applies a comparative analytical framework using compact electro-thermal models to examine the state-dependent readout and programming behavior.
model_or_system: The physical system is the disc-type PCM device, modeled using electro-thermal equations that govern Joule heating during RESET/SET operations. The analysis involves deriving resistance components based on amorphous and crystalline phases and modeling thermal resistance ($R_{th}$).
key_observables: Total device resistance ($R$), programming current ($I_{	ext{prog}}$), power dissipation ($\dot{Q}$), and temperature rise ($\Delta T_{	ext{hot}}$).
important_parameters: Bottom electrode radius ($r_{	ext{BE}}$), phase-change material radius ($r_{	ext{PCM}}$), amorphous radius ($u_a$), and the adiabatic programming limit.
main_assumptions: Assumes the system reduces to a two-dimensional geometry ($t_{	ext{PCM}} \le 10 	ext{ nm}$) and neglects charge accumulation during steady-state readout.
figures_summary: Figures compare disc-type PCM with other architectures, show resistance dependence on amorphous extent ($u_a$), and compare scaling against the adiabatic limit and SRAM cells.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical model, deriving analytical expressions for resistance and thermal response, comparing disc vs. dome geometries, analyzing scaling limits, and concluding with performance metrics for IMC.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state memory, the detailed electro-thermal modeling, phase transition physics, and scaling analysis involve non-equilibrium thermodynamics and transport phenomena that share mathematical rigor with open quantum system dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Disc-type Phase Change Memory. (A) The top panel shows a schematic cross-sectional view of a disc-type device. The device features a vertical structure, with an ultra-thin (≤10 nm) phase-change material layer positioned between the dielectric and bottom electrode. Top contact is made laterally at the outer edge of the phase-change layer. Based on the fabrication design, the bottom electrode can form either a planar contact or an edge contact with the phase-change material. In both cases, the current flows radially through the device. Compared to 3D dome-type configurations in prototypical devices, such as the mushroom cell (bottom panel), the amorphous regions form spatially...

FIG. 2. Read Characteristics. (A) The device resistance as a function of the amorphous extent (ua) for disc-type and dome-type geometries, computed using the analytical model. In disc-type devices, current always traverses the amorphous region regardless of its size, whereas in dome-type geometries this occurs only once the amorphous volume fully covers the bottom electrode (for ua ≥rb.e). The scatter points represent resistance values obtained using finite-element simulations, showing a good agreement with the analytical model. (B) Variation in RESET resistance due to fabrication-induced variability in the bottom-electrode radius, rBE. The radius is sampled from a Gaussian distribution...

FIG. 3. RESET Characteristics. (A) Comparison of power density between disc-type and dome-type geometries, illustrating heat generation efficiency in the devices. Disc-type cells exhibit improved power density. (B) Thermal resistance of disc-type devices for various sizes of melt volumes. The inset shows a similar plot for a dome-type geometry. Notably, the absolute values of Rth are increased, and its spatial dependency is reduced in disc-type devices. (C) Programming-current dependence of the phase-change region in disc-type devices with 3 and 5 nm GST. Solid curves show the analytical electrothermal model, symbols represent FEM results, and dashed curves are stretched-exponential fits....

FIG. 4. Threshold Switching Characteristics. (A) Comparison of threshold field for different thermal resistance values. The logarithmic field dependence indicates higher voltages are required for switching. The dotted vertical lines are experimental values of activation energies of GST, with and without spaital confinement. (B) Computed threshold voltage characteristics as a function of amorphous volume in the disc and dome-type device geometries, showing a difference in their dependencies. The inset show the full current-voltage behavior of a full RESET state, highlighting the improved thermal resistance to be a key property in disc-type devices.

FIG. 5. Endurance characteristics. (A) Experimental Rdynamic as a function of programming current for a disc-type device, together with the fit obtained from the analytical model. (B) Magnitude of the relative variation in Rdynamic resulting from variations in the bottom-electrode radius rBE for disc- and dome-type phase configurations. (C) Magnitude of the relative variation in Rdynamic resulting from variations in the molten- and crystalline-state resistivities, ρmelt and ρcrys, for the two device geometries. The geometrical and material variations serve as proxies for structural and compositional changes that may develop during extensive cyclic stressing.
